newsitem.title: INDIA: Regional leaders strong in India leadership race.
newsitem.headline: Regional leaders strong in India leadership race.

text.p: Regional Tamil leader G.K. Moopanar and foreign minister Inder Kumar Gujral were seen as possible successors for Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda on Monday as India's ousted coalition pondered a new government.

Politicians also said they were keenly watching Telugu Desam Party (TDP) leader Chandrababu Naidu, the youthful convenor of the 15-party United Front, even though he has asserted that he is not in the race for the prermiership.
"It is not that he is not there. He is playing his cards safely," a senior coalition leader, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters.

He said Industry Minister Murasoli Maran of southern Tamil Nadu state's Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) party and the Janata Dal's Gujral were among other contenders to head a government aimed at avoiding mid-term elections.

The centre-left alliance said on Sunday it was willing to consider a replacement for Deve Gowda to make a fresh deal with the Congress party, which on March 30 withdrew critical support for the coalition in a fragmented parliament.
The Press Trust of India reported that the United Front's decision-making Steering Committee is scheduled to choose its new leader on Thursday.
Analysts said that it was clear that regional allies forming the backbone of the 10-month-old coalition would call the shots rather than Deve Gowda's Janata Dal party.
"It is very difficult to tell (who the new leader is). The bottom line is that regional parties are important," said Mahesh Rangarajan of the Centre for Contemporary Studies.
The Congress ousted the coalition in a confidence vote on Friday after it rejected a demand that Deve Gowda, whom it accused of not containing Hindu nationalists, must resign for support to resume.
Deve Gowda favours fresh elections, but regional allies who do not want new polls have prevailed over him.
Key questions will have to be resolved before the political parties can decide who will rule India next.
"It has to be someone who others won't be threatened by," Rangarajan said.
From this point of view, foreign minister Gujral, a mild-mannered man with no political base to speak of, could be a choice, he said. "A political lightweight is easier," he said.
The goateed leader has been instrumental in India's signing a landmark water-sharing treaty with Bangladesh and reviving talks to ease ties with arch-rival Pakistan.

Rangarajan said G.K. Moopanar, leader of the Tamil Manila Congress (TMC), or his party lieutenant, Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, could be the group's choice. But he added that Moopanar's proximity to the Congress party could hurt him.

The two leaders broke away to form the new party last year following differences with then prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao over election allies. But Rao has since been replaced as the Congress party's president.
"Ten Janpath wants Moopanar," said a minister, referring to the address of Sonia Gandhi, the influential Italian-born widow of former prime minister and Congress leader Rajiv Gandhi.
Moopanar, a chain-smoking gentleman farmer from Tamil Nadu, was for decades a key Gandhi family aide and party strategist.

Telugu Desam's Naidu is believed to have officially dropped from the race because he does not want to risk staking a strong leadership in his home state to lead a federal government that may not last long.
In New Delhi, political pundits believe that the Congress can easily topple another coalition formed with its support, as it has already done thrice in independent India's history.
Rangarajan said the Janata Dal's Ram Vilas Paswan, currently railway minister, could be a surprise candidate, as he was a popular leader from the lowest of Hindu castes.
